input.question: If someone receives a full organ transplant will the organ be eventually replaced by the host's cells or will it remain as the the donor's cells for the rest of the host's life.
input.ground_truth: It will always be the donor's cells. It can be possible to wean off of antirejection drugs as your body gets used to the new organ, but if your whole liver is replaced by a donor liver, you do not have any of your own liver cells to replicate and replace the donor cells.

response.prediction:
Okay, let’s imagine you have a toy car, and your friend gives you a brand new toy car engine to put inside it. Now, your toy car looks and works great with the new engine from your friend.

But, your body is a little bit like the toy car, and the new organ (like a heart or kidney) is like your friend’s engine. The new organ is made of your friend’s special tiny building blocks called “cells.”

Now, here’s the interesting part: Your body’s own tiny workers (called immune cells) try to fix or change things that aren’t from you. But the cells in the new organ are protected in a special way, so they usually stay as your friend’s cells for a long, long time—maybe even your whole life.

However, sometimes, over many, many years, a few of your own body’s cells might slowly sneak in and replace some of the donor’s cells. But most of the organ will still have your friend’s cells for a very long time.

So, the new organ mostly stays as your friend’s cells, but a tiny bit might change over many, many years.
